idiom_name: two role objects (acceptor/connector) + handler factory + dispatcher hand-off
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give the service a passive role (bind/listen/accept loop) and an active role (resolve/dial), each ending in a single hand-off step that instantiates the service handler, injects the connected endpoint and calls its activation hook. Keep the mapping service id -> handler in a factory/registry so the roles stay closed for modification. Drive acceptance and connection completion through the runtime's event demultiplexer (readiness- or completion-based) instead of one thread per connection whenever connection counts are high. The handler must never touch the listening endpoint; it owns only the connected endpoint.
code_sketch:
acceptor.bind(endpoint)
loop:
    conn = dispatcher.wait_for_incoming()          # readiness- or completion-based
    handler = factory.create(service_id(conn))
    handler.activate(conn)                         # init + register with dispatcher
# connector:
conn = dial(endpoint); handler = factory.create(...); handler.activate(conn)
pitfalls: Wrong: let the acceptor parse messages after accept -> setup and service logic become coupled again, so a transport change edits handler code -> Instead: hand each connected endpoint to a fresh handler and dispatcher.

Wrong: reuse one mutable handler across connections -> per-connection authentication, buffers or session state leak between peers -> Instead: create one handler instance per connection or prove complete state isolation.

Wrong: accept without bounds on backlog, handshakes or active handlers -> connection storms exhaust file descriptors, memory or CPU before service code can run -> Instead: combine backlog sizing with admission limits and bounded handshake concurrency.

Wrong: run blocking TLS, certificate loading or handler construction on the acceptor's event-loop thread -> one slow setup stalls all new connections -> Instead: bound setup and offload blocking work before activation.
Wrong: close the listener and active handlers in one shutdown step -> in-flight clients see resets and retry storms -> Instead: stop accepting, drain handlers with a deadline, then close resources.

Wrong: let many workers wake on one shared listener -> thundering-herd wakeups waste CPU and produce EAGAIN races -> Instead: designate an acceptor, use EPOLLEXCLUSIVE, or use separate SO_REUSEPORT listeners.
